caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 229 of 2007 with Civil Rule No. 665 (FM) of 2006.
lawyer:
Mf Farooque with AFM Ashaduzzaman and Nazneen Nahar Advocates-----For Appellants. 
Khalilur Rahman with TM Shakil Hasan and Md. Khalilur Rahman (Helal), Advocates-----For the Respondents.
parties:
Joinal Abedin Jamal and others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Noor Afza ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J : This appeal has been preferred by the 2nd party appellants being aggrieved by Order No.37 dated 2S-3-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 973 of 2002 refusing to set aside the arbitral award dated 11-6-2003 passed by the sole Arbitrator. Facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal in short are that the appellants being owners of, approximately, 18.40 kathas of land, comprising of Dhaka City Corporation holdings No. 80, 80/1, 80/2 and 80/3, Nowabpur, within Sutrapur Police station, fully described in the Agreement (Bainapatra) (subsequently described as the arbitral agreement), executed between the appellants and the present respondent on 4-8-1999 for sale of the said property at a consideration of Taka 3,68,00,000. As per terms of the said agreement, the present respondent was suppose to pay Taka 50,00,000 to the appellants as advance. Accordingly, the respondent paid Taka 2,50,000 in cash, Taka 35,00,000 in cheque dated 4-8-1999 of lslami Bank and the rest of Taka 12,50,000 by another cheque of AI-Baraka Bank (BD) Limited dated 11-8-1999. It was further contemplated in the said agreement that since the sellers(appellants) mortgaged the property in question with Islami Bank (BD) Ltd. prior to the said agreement, sale deed cannot be executed and registered without releasing the property from the said Bank upon repaying the entire loan. But, however, according to the terms of the agreement, possession in a portion of the said property was handed over to the purchaser respondent who was also allowed to put up a signboard in her own name upon expressing willingness to sell/allot different spaces for market/office/apartment/car parking to the interested persons. The purchaser respondent was also allowed to obtain clearance certificate from the RAJUK and get the plan approved and sale/allot the aforementioned spaces to various customers and receive money for the said purpose from the aspirant customers. The seller appellants under the said agreement were bound to assist the purchaser respondent in all respect. In. case the seller appellants would not co-operate with the purchaser in respect of the works mentioned above, the seller would be wholly responsible for the damages arising out of such non- co-operation. Under such circumstances, it is alleged by the respondent, that the seller- appellants, in violation of the terms of the said agreement did not handover the possession of the entire property along with all original documents upon executing the sale deed even upon receiving Taka 37,5.0,000 in advance for which the purchaser respondent, on various occasions requested the seller appellants, through her agent, to hand over the possession of the entire property along with all original papers. But the seller appellants did not comply with the same. Thus the purchaser respondent, on the basis of Clause No.6 of the said agreement gave a notice on 05.08.2002 to the seller appellants for arbitration upon appointing Mr. AFM Mesbahuddin, a former Judge of the High Court Division, as her Arbitrator and requested the seller appellants to appoint their Arbitrator within 30 days from the date of service of the said notice failing which the purchaser respondent would have no alternative but to take shelter of the Court under the existing law. The seller appellants received the said notice on 6-8-2002 but did not comply with the same. Thus the purchaser respondent, on 19-11-2002, filed an application before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 12(3)(1)(ka) of the Arbitration Act 2001 (which came into force upon repealing the earlier Act of 1940), for appointment of Arbitrator. 

 6. He next submits that although section 17 of the Act, 2001, described the jurisdiction of the arbitral Tribunal and 17(kha) specifically gave authority to the arbitral Tribunal to give decision on the question of its proper constitution/composition/ appointment, yet the aggrieved party can take the said plea for cancellation of the award under section 42 and 43 of the said Act, as the same has given a statutory relief in section 43. Then he submits that although the general principle of law is that the question as to jurisdiction or objection to jurisdiction is to be taken at the earliest stage, even then any party having not taken such objection earlier, can take such objection as a ground for cancellation of the award as provided in section 43(1)(ক)(উ) when such question affects the decision of the Arbitrator. In this respect he referred to section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure as a principle of statute. Lastly, he submits that the learned District Judge, by appointing the nominee of the respondent as the sole Arbitrator, has committed illegality which is malice in law. As such, the appointment is contrary to the arbitration agreement. Thus the sole Arbitrator being not a neutral person the award passed by him is liable to be cancelled. In support of this submissions he relied on the cases of Hazrat Ali vs Election Commission, reported in 41 DLR 486; Darbari Lal Mudi vs Raneeganj Coal Association Ltd, reported in AIR (31) 1944 (Patna) 30; in Waverly Jute Mills Co. Ltd, vs Raymon and Company India (Pvt) Ltd (and connected appeals), reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 90 = 1963 (3) SCR 209 (judgment delivered on 4-5-1962 in Civil Appeal Nos. 389 to 392 of 1960) and also in the case of Khardah Company Limited vs Raymon and Company (India) Private Limited reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 1810 (Judgment delivered on 4-5-1962 in Civil Appeal Nos. 98 and 99 of 1960). 

 7. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the purchaser respondent submits that the present Arbitration Act, 2001 is a consolidated statute which contains both procedural and substantive law dealing with different subjects at different stages under different chapters. According to him, the well settled principle in the legal arena is "objection as to jurisdiction/ constitution of a Court/ Tribunal is to be taken at the preliminary stage, before the same Court! Tribunal on the earliest possible opportunity." Thus section 6, under chapter II of the Act provides if such objection is not taken at the right time then it will be deemed that the said party has waived his right as to the same. Again chapter -IV (section 11 to 16) deals with appointment of Arbitrator, objection to appointment and appeal against any order as to appointment. Thus in the present case, if the appellants had any objection against the appointment of the sole Arbitrator under section 12 of the Act then they had opportunity to raise such objection against such appointment under section 13 and 14 of the Act. The appellants also had opportunity to raise such objection before the Arbitrator himself, as section 17 provides power to the Arbitrator / Tribunal, itself to decide any question as to its appointment/ constitution/ composition and section 19 provides the right to any party to the arbitration to raise such objection before filing the statement of claim or objection against the same whereupon the Tribunal is to give decision on such objection, raised before it. The Act under section 20, provides forum to challenge the decision of the Arbitrator before the High Court Division. Thus he submits that the appellants had a series of opportunity to challenge the appointment but having not availed any of the aforesaid forums provided under sections, 13, 14, 17, 19 and 20 of the Act it is clear that they have not only waived their right to raise such question, under section 6 but also are estoppel from doing so at a belated stage like after the completion of the arbitration proceedings and passing of the award. Relying on the well settled principle that 'a person cannot take advantage of his own wrong'; meaning a person, who did not avail the opportunity earlier is stopped from taking such objection at subsequent stage, as the appellants waived their right now they cannot take the same plea before any forum after the finality of the proceeding. 

 8. Referring to the case of Sree Sudhir Chandra Saha vs Matiran Bewa reported in 6 BLD (AD) 182, Mr. Rahman submits that when any party's conduct is in contravention to the well settled principle embodied in the legal maxim that 'no man shall take advantage of his own wrong' the plea of estoppel would be available to bar investigation of a question of fact about which a representation had been made so as to induce the other party to change his position to his prejudice and thus the principle that there being no estoppel against a statute', should only be invoked in such cases, when on the face of it, the contract is shown to be tainted with illegality. He next submits that in the present case the contract being not tainted with any illegality rather there being a valid contract, as the parties admittedly agreed to arbitrate the dispute and the Arbitrator having been appointed by the Court without any objection raised by either party against such appointment and the parties having entered appearance before the said Arbitrator and proceeded with the arbitration without any question as to the constitution/ appointment! jurisdiction of the arbitral Tribunal, the appellant now cannot take advantage of his own wrong upon taking advantage of the principle " there is no estoppel against statute" which cannot be invoked in this case. Lastly, Mr. Rahman submits that the question raised herein is a mere technicality, which will not stand in the way of a decision unless the decision appears to be illegal or apparently the decision is liable to be set aside. He submits that the award has been passed on the basis of admitted facts that the respondent paid and the appellants received Taka 37,50,000 as such the appellants were directed to repay/return the same amount to the respondent of course with 6% interest thereon. Thus, no evidence/paper having been filed by the appellants to show that the award passed is tainted with illegality, there will be no change in the decision, even if, the allegation as to technicality in appointing the Arbitrator is found to be not in accordance with law, is taken into consideration. Thus the decision neither appears to be illegal nor apparently the same is liable to be set aside. Mr. Rahman submits that the aforesaid principle could be invoked only in a case of inherent lack of jurisdiction, when consent or waiver cannot confer jurisdiction, as decided in the case of the Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh vs Md Shafiuddin reported in 10 BLT (AD) 50. But in the present case there is no inherent lack of jurisdiction for which the appellant could take advantage of the said decision. 

 9. In support of his above contentions apart from the aforesaid decision, Mr. Rahman also relied on the cases of Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute vs Mr. Bhuiyan Ltd, reported in 61 DLR 400; Bangladesh Water Development Board and others, vs Progati Prakaushali reported in 49 DLR 335; Sree Sudhir Chandra Saha vs Matiran Bewa being dead her heirs Nazmul Rahman Sarker, reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 182; AIR 1945 (Bom) 497 (In re All India Groundnut Syndicate Ltd), Gopal Krishna Das vs Abdul Kader Mia reported in 35 DLR 14; Nagendra Nath Sen Roy vs Saiyad Ali Jamadar, reported in 8 DLR 100; on the case of Abdus Samad Paramanik vs Mosammat Bilkis Khatun reported in BSCD Vol-VI Page 53; The Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh vs Md Shafiuddin reported in 10 BLT (AD) 50; Chief Kwame asante Tredehene vs Chief Kwame Tawia reported in 9 DLR 686; Muhammad Saghir Bhatti and Sons vs Federation of Pakistan, reported in 10 DLR (SC) 169 and in the case of Pubali Bank Ltd vs Contech Ltd. reported in 27 BLD 133. Thus he submits that considering the facts of the case and the principle laid down in the above decisions the appeal is liable to be dismissed with costs. 

 10. Heard the learned advocates, perused the record and the decisions referred above. On perusal of the record, it appears that the learned District Judge, upon perusing the papers filed by both the parties and upon hearing the parties, appointed Mr. AFM Meshbauddin, the Arbitrator to arbitrate the dispute between the parties in accordance with Arbitration Act 2001 by his order No.5 dated 6-3-2003 and directed the Arbitrator to submit the award in the said Court by 7-5-2003 which was subsequently extended till 11-6-2003 by order dated 5.5.2003 on the prayer of the parties. Thereafter, the said Arbitrator entered into the reference and accordingly, Arbitration Case No. 1 of 2003 was commenced. By Order No. 1 dated 6-4-2003 the Arbitrator, notified the parties and directed them to appear before him and produce all necessary papers and documents, by 10-4-2003. Upon receipt of such notices the parties appeared before the sole Arbitrator and fi led their respective claims, and counter claims along with all supporting papers. It appears from the record that the seller-appellants filed their claim before the Arbitrator on 13-5-2003, without raising any objection as to the appointment or as to the Arbitrator's jurisdiction. Rather it appears that they prayed for passing an award of Taka 6,28,80,000 in their favour. The purchaser respondent on 24-5-2003, filed written objection against the said claim of the seller appellants denying the allegations made therein and on the contrary prayed for an award in her favour claiming Taka 70,00,000 along with interests at the rate of 16% per annum on the said amount till realisation of the same. The learned Arbitrator upon considering the evidences, both oral and documentary, adduced by the parties passed the award dated 11-6-2003, which is under challenge in this appeal. However, since the learned advocate for the appellants admits that he cannot and as such shall not argue on merit of the award but he will simply argue on the appointment and jurisdiction of the Arbitrator so the point, in the instant appeal, for determination is whether the appointment of the sole Arbitrator under section 12 of the Act by the learned District Judge can be called in question after the award is passed upon hearing the parties, without any objection on such question being raised any time before the Tribunal and whether the Arbitrator had jurisdiction to pass the award in question, which has been challenged herein under section 42/43 of the Act. 

 12. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law it is very clear that any objection as to appointment, jurisdiction or neutrality and independence of the Arbitrator is required to be taken at the earliest opportunity if not before any forum but before the Arbitrator himself prior to filing their respective claims, under section 14(2) and the Arbitrator upon receiving such objection is duty bound to give decision on the same within 30 days from the date of filing of such objection as provided in section 14(3). If any party is aggrieved by such decision he has a right to prefer appeal before the High Court Division under section 14(4) within 30 days of the date of such decision and the High Court Division will give decision on the matter within 90 days of filing of the appeal as provided in section 14(5). Section 15 also provides right to the parties to apply for removal of the Arbitrator through Court. Moreover, under section 17 the arbitral Tribunal has the power to decide any question, including its own jurisdiction and also to decide whether the constitution has been made is accordance with law. Again section 19(1) clearly provides that any objection as to jurisdiction/appointment is to be raised before the arbitral Tribunal before filing of the written objection and section 19(2) provides for raising objection as to exceeding his authority to be taken immediately during the course of continuation of the proceeding. Section 19(3) provides for condonation of delay in filing the aforesaid objections and under section 19(4) the Tribunal is duly bound to give decision on such objections. Section 20 provides for moving the High Court Division for remedy in case any party is aggrieved by the decision given under section 19. 

 14. In the present appeal, since after the appointment of the Arbitrator the appellant got opportunity to raise objection as to appointment and / or jurisdiction of the Arbitrator but did not raise any objection, whatsoever, at the appropriate time nor they availed the opportunity under section 19(3) or before any other forum rather participated in the proceeding resulting in passing of the award, they, under section 6 of the Act, have waived the right to raise such objection by their conduct and acquiescence and as such estoppel in law from challenging the validity of the reference as well as the award. In the case of Fisheries Research Institute vs MR Bhuiyan Ltd., (61 DLR 400) a Division Bench of this Court held that the point of jurisdiction depending upon the determination of this contentions question of fact between the parties which manifests a go-by by the party by joining in the petition to the Court asking it to make a reference to arbitration and further by taking part in the proceedings before the Arbitrator. Thus it is not open to the said party now to turn around and say that the Arbitrator has no jurisdiction. Moreover, objection as to jurisdiction being "technical" in nature, the same is not tenable at a belated stage. This view finds support in the case of Coal Controller vs Ventura Industries Ltd, reported in 45 DLR (AD)183 where the apex Court observed that this objection is a technical objection which the petitioner could have raised before. Thus when the Arbitrator has already entered on the reference and has started issuing notices to the parties the Court held we 'are not inclined to entertain this technical objection at this stage. In the present appeal the appellants did not raise any objection at any stage before any forum and they allowed the Arbitrator to complete the proceeding and pass the award. So having regard to the aforesaid decisions their objection at such belated stage is not at all maintainable in law. Again in the case of Adamjee Sons Ltd. vs Jibon Bima Corporation, reported in 45 DLR 89 it has been held that where the parties submit to the arbitration and making prayer for passing the award, such parties cannot be allowed to take objection as to the validity of the award on the ground of want of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator. In the case of Pakistan Trading Company vs MM Ispahani Ltd, reported in 11 DLR 405 it has been held that when the petitioner submitted to the Arbitrator with his eyes wide open and knowing fully well that the particular Arbitrator is a member of the arbitration, it is not now open to him to say that he has got a reasonable apprehension that he will not get a proper and fair trial before the said Arbitrator. Thus, in the present case, the appellants, admittedly, having not taken any objection, whatsoever, before the Arbitrator and such action of the appellants having led the other side to believe that such right will not be enforced they are now precluded from taking any such objection at a belated stage like after passing of the award on contest. This view finds support in the case of Ocean lndustries Ltd. and another vs Industrial Development Bank, reported in 18 DLR (SC) 354. Again, in the case of Pathumma vs Kuntaklan Kutty, reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 1683 and in the case of Pakistan vs Abdul Kuddus, reported in PLD 1961(Dacca) 616, it has been held that objection as to jurisdiction can be allowed at the appellate stage if three conditions are fulfilled they are: (i) The objection was taken in the Court of first instance (ii) it was taken at the earliest possible opportunity and in case where issues are settled at or before such settlement; and (iii) there has been a consequent failure of justice. But the appellants have miserably failed to show that their case falls within any of the above noted conditions. 

 16. From a reading of the aforesaid statutory provision of section 43(1)(ক)(উ) it appears that the appellants are required to make out a case that the constitution/appointment of the arbitral Tribunal or the arbitration proceeding was not consistent with the arbitration agreement. But nothing as such has been made out or proved by the appellants in that manner anywhere at the earliest stage. Though the said provision provides for filing an application for cancellation of the award on the ground of constitution/Jurisdiction but the general principle as settled by the superior Courts categorically say that such objection is required to be taken at the initial stage and then when such objection, raised before the Arbitrator challenging his appointment/jurisdiction, has been failed and/or in case the Arbitrator, proceeded with the arbitration inspite of such objection having been raised before him and rejected, and passed an award, only then the aggrieved party can take such objection as a ground for cancellation of the award under section 43(1)(ক)(উ). Otherwise the provisions of sections 6, 13, 14, 15 and 17 will be redundant. In the present case since the appellants did not avail the opportunity of raising any such objection at the initial stage before the Arbitrator himself which gave an impression to the respondent that they would not avail the right of objection as to appointment/jurisdiction and thereby allowed the proceeding to be completed as such, now, we are of the view, that such objection cannot be taken at a belated stage as a ground for cancellation of the award passed on contest. If that be allowed then the appellants would be given a chance to take advantage of their own wrong done earlier by not taking proper step at proper time as decided by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 6 BLD (AD) 182 referred earlier. It is true that there is no estoppel against statute. But question is whether this principle can be invoked by one to take advantage of his own wrong/ fraud, to the detriment of the other party, who was given a bonafide belief,. by not invoking the right at the proper time, that the right to raise such objection has been waived. The said principle as to "no estoppel against statute," can only be attracted when the statute appears to defeat the public policy not in the present case where a private interest is involved under no circumstances can be attracted to defeat the public policy as appears from the facts and circumstances discussed above. Thus in the instant case the submissions of the learned advocate for the appellants that "there is no estoppel against the statute" is not tenable.
